title: Bridge Runway: Stabilization Sprint Playbook (2027)
body:
Summary:
The Stabilization Sprint is a short, focused incident flow for regional or multi-region degradations that put SLOs at risk but can be recovered through coordinated remediation within roughly 2–6 hours. The emphasis is fast containment, careful tactical rollouts, customer-safe messaging and a clean handoff to post-incident work.

When to use it:
- A region or major capacity pool shows measurable SLO drift (see thresholds).
- Recovery is expected inside a working-day sprint (<= 6 hours) and no P0 legal/compliance escalation is needed.
- Do not use it for silent data integrity or security incidents; those follow the security/IR runbooks.

Trigger thresholds:
- Availability: region availability under 99.9% over the last 15m AND customer error rate > 2x baseline for > 10m.
- Latency: hosted API p95 generation latency > 1s, or p99 > 2s depending on model class.
- Throughput: request queue sustained > 30% above provisioned burst capacity for 15m.

Roles:
- Bridge Conductor (owner): runs the sprint, keeps time, owns customer/status messaging.
- Tier-1 Responder: first diagnostics and mitigations (restart shards, clear KV cache, revert canary).
- Service Steward: domain expert who validates hypotheses and approves fallbacks/rollouts.
- Capacity Lead: Dedicated/Private capacity moves, scaling, capacity masking.
- Customer Liaison: status page posts and direct comms to impacted accounts.
- Incident Scribe: chronology and evidence in the incident dossier.

Readiness checklist:
- Bridge call open and Slack channel #incident-bridge created.
- Dashboards, alert links, hotfix playbooks and rollback procedures at hand.
- Short-term quotas cleared; eviction/queue flushing runbooks accessible.
- Named role assignments recorded in the bridge header.

Sprint timeline:
0-10 minutes — Kickoff
1. Bridge Conductor opens the bridge and states scope, impact, SLOs at risk and role owners.
2. Tier-1 Responder contains: fallback model variants, pause background batch jobs, apply circuit breakers.
3. Customer Liaison posts the first internal and public status and flags high-touch customers.

10-30 minutes — Evidence and first mitigations
1. Pull traces, p95/p99 latency buckets, GPU saturation and queue depth; save JSON from the metrics collector.
2. Service Steward decides whether a hotfix (kernel parameter, config flip, scaling policy) is viable.
3. Capacity Lead weighs adding reserved nodes or shifting burst traffic across regions, noting warm-up time.

30-90 minutes — Controlled remediation
1. Use the lowest-risk path: canary on <10% of traffic with 30m bake windows.
2. Roll back with the command set in the Appendix if needed.
3. Check impact every 5 minutes; update the bridge every 10 minutes.

90-240 minutes — Recovery and closure
1. Recovery means availability >= SLO for 15m, normal p95 latency and falling queue depth.
2. Once stable, move the bridge to monitoring-only and plan the handoff.
3. If it is not stabilizing, move to a sustained incident with exec notification.

Customer communications:
- Initial public status:
  "We are investigating increased latency for requests in <region>. Some customers may see slower responses. Engineers are working on a mitigation. Updates every 15 minutes."
- Post-mitigation update:
  "We applied a targeted mitigation that reduced error rates and latency for affected requests. We continue to monitor and will contact impacted customers directly as needed."
- High-touch email:
  Subject: Service impact in <region> — update
  Body: Hello <Customer>, we saw elevated latency and errors for requests routed to <region>. A mitigation applied at <time UTC> restored performance for most traffic. We are monitoring and will share a full post-incident report. For urgent help, reply here or contact <CS-Pager>.

Status page: use the unified status page fields incident_id, short_description, impact, start_time, current_status, next_update ETA. Keep messages high-level, no speculative root causes.

Change decision checklist:
- Reversible within the bake window?
- Reduces customer-facing errors in canary?
- Blast radius limited to a known tenant set or region?
- Approved by the Service Steward? If not, hold and keep mitigating.

Escalation:
- If SLOs are not trending back within 3 hours, escalate to the Executive War Room and bring in PM/CS leads.
- Any data loss or incorrect outputs go straight to the Security & Compliance incident path.

Handoff and postmortem:
- Bridge Conductor opens a postmortem ticket, assigns owners and schedules a retro within 48–72h.
- Required artifacts: timeline, metric snapshots, failed runbook actions, customer comms log.
- Postmortem must cover summary, timeline, root cause hypothesis, corrective actions (owner + ETA) and prevention.

Game day (quarterly):
- Simulate a regional degradation end-to-end with all six roles.
- Scenarios: saturated GPU cluster, KV cache eviction storm, rollout causing p99 spikes.
- Success: bridge up in <=5 minutes, first mitigation in <=15 minutes, canary and rollback exercised, customer message out within 10 minutes.
- Deliverables: short retro, runbook updates, improvement items in the sprint backlog.

Appendix: commands
- Rollback: kubectl -n inference rollout undo deployment/model-service --to-revision=<rev>
- Cache flush: redwood-cli cache flush --service model-service --region <region> --prefix kv-prefix
- Metrics query: curl -s "https://metrics.internal/api/query?expr=llm_request_p95&start=<t0>&end=<t1>" | jq .

Evidence checklist:
- Keep raw traces and span IDs for 30 days on the incident ticket.
- Export dashboard snapshots as PNGs into the dossier.
- Record impacted customer buckets and keep request IDs for reconciliation.

Ownership:
- Owned by Eng SRE. Reviewed annually and after every stabilization sprint.
- Contact: eng-sre-runbooks@redwood.ai

Last reviewed by: Marcus Lee, Jillian Park
